prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active forms, which made possible incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B033 alone, credited to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange did not move me, because no member challenged the science or the maturity of the work. The chain from incretin physiology and proglucagon processing, through the identity of the active truncated peptide and receptor biology, to drugs with large randomized outcome trials in diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal disease, is original, independently confirmed and mature. A prize for the mechanism is the better fit for Physiology or Medicine, and the citation names the therapies that followed without making them the award. On the chair's question, I regard the achievement as the physiology, with the drugs as its demonstration. I considered a two-part prize with CAR-T, but it would cut the GLP-1 part to one name and force a cut among Holst, Drucker and Mojsov, whose roles are clearer than any CAR-T allocation I can defend. I would not accept that cost.
statement.case_against: The credit remains the weak point. I cannot settle Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide against Habener and colleagues from the supplied text, and Habener is outside the credited names. I keep Mojsov because her identification and synthesis of the active peptide is distinct and enabled the pharmacology, but that is a judgement under uncertainty and I state it as such. Leaving out Knudsen is a deliberate choice the committee should record as one, since her medicinal chemistry produced liraglutide and semaglutide. If the committee concludes that the drugs are the achievement, this configuration is the wrong one and should be reconsidered openly, not by quiet substitution.

responses.point: Perlmann says rewarding translation is not alien to the prize when it rests on a discovery, and would keep Knudsen as the point to revisit if Mojsov's priority cannot be defended.
responses.response: I accept that translation can be rewarded, but I would not make Knudsen the automatic fallback if Mojsov's claim weakened. The question is whether the active-peptide discovery stands, and the nomination text cannot settle it, so the honest statement is that I hold Mojsov on the strength of identification and synthesis of the active form, not on a resolved priority. If that claim were shown to belong mainly to others who are not credited, I would want an explicit decision about the third slot, with Knudsen as one option, not a quiet swap. On the UPR, I take his point that its link to practice is indirect, which is why I keep B048 only as an alternative this year.

responses.point: The chair asks whether the GLP-1 achievement is the physiology or the drug development, and whether a two-part prize is acceptable if the cap cuts the GLP-1 part below three names.
responses.response: My answer is that the achievement is the physiology, which is why Knudsen has no slot in my configuration, and the citation says incretin-based therapies were made possible by it. On the two-part question, I would not pay the cost. A second part with CAR-T needs two names, June and Sadelain, which leaves one name for GLP-1, and no single credit there is defensible. I agree with the chair that the Mojsov versus Habener question is a gap in the record. Where I differ slightly is that I would not treat it as a reason to wait for a later year, because the physiology of Holst and Drucker is secure whatever the answer on the peptide.

responses.point: El Manira ranks optogenetics third and says the six-name problem on B007 cannot be settled on priority alone.
responses.response: I agree that the six-name problem on B007 is the main obstacle, since any trio of Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann leaves out Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck. I also still see optogenetics as a tool whose medical translation is limited to early retinal work, so it stays behind B026 and B048 for me. If the committee did want a neuroscience tool prize, Nagel and Hegemann's channelrhodopsin discovery as the original contribution, with Deisseroth's demonstration in neurons, is the defensible core, but I would want the omissions recorded.

responses.point: Linnarsson keeps BCR-ABL inhibition (B032) as an alternative for its decades of survival data and describes it as arguably overdue.
responses.response: I accept that imatinib is a paradigm of targeted therapy with decades of follow-up, and that overdue is a fair description of its place in oncology. I still read B032 as an application of earlier oncogene and kinase biology, with the credited names recognised for drug development, resistance and clinical proof, so I keep it out of my alternatives. If the committee chose it, I would want the citation to name the clinical demonstration as the achievement, and not claim the discovery of the target. I would also want the earlier oncogene chain, outside the credited names, addressed before any ballot.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks TNF blockade second and notes that incretin therapy may already attract so much attention that the committee should check it is not following popularity.
responses.response: I share the concern about popularity and tested the case against it. The case for B033 does not depend on public attention, since the physiology was established decades ago and the outcome trials are independent. On B051 I still rank it low because the TNF biology (Cerami, Vilcek, Kollias) lies outside Feldmann and Maini. I accept that it would be a clean pair and I do not dispute the clinical effect. If a second achievement were ever added, her IL-6 comparison would have to be dealt with at the same time.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide against Habener and colleagues supports her inclusion; the supplied text does not resolve it.
Whether the committee regards the achievement as physiology or drug development, since the three-person cap forces the Knudsen exclusion.
Whether any CAR-T configuration from the supplied names is fair given Eshhar's chimeric receptor concept and Rosenberg's separate adoptive cell therapy line.
I rely on my own recall of several priority histories (Habener, Eshhar, TNF and oncogene work), which I have not verified against external sources.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My profile documents co-authorship with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisén and joint work with Christopher Burge's group at MIT. None of them is credited on a shortlisted ballot, and I have no documented involvement with any shortlisted candidate or any credited name. Shared KI affiliation is not treated as a conflict. Nothing in the round-1 statements or the chair's summary changes this.
